st.headline: Wall Street closes lower to end rocky week
st.teaser: The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16.
fullText: NEW YORK - Wall Street’s main indexes closed lower on Oct 23 even as technology shares steadied somewhat to end a turbulent week for the market-driving AI trade, and investors looked ahead to a busy slate of corporate earnings and a Federal Reserve interest-rate policy meeting.
The Nasdaq Composite posted a slim loss a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest one-day drop since June, as concerns flared over financing costs to support heavy AI investment spending.
The S&P 500 technology sector posted a 0.35% gain on Oct 23.
Most S&P 500 sectors fell, however, including declines of well over 1% for the consumer staples and consumer discretionary groups as well as the financials sector.

Next week, about one-third of S&P 500 companies report quarterly results, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, three AI hyperscalers whose capital spending forecasts will be closely watched on Wall Street.

“There is still fallout from the questioning of the AI trade,” said Kristina Hooper, chief market strategist at Man Group. “There’s certainly the potential that we see less invested in an AI data centre build-out next year than has been projected. So I certainly think that’s giving pause.”
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23%, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 lost 39.75 points, or 0.52%, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 53.52 points, or 0.21%, to 25,955.34.
For the week, the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the Nasdaq dropped 0.7%.
The blue-chip Dow rose 0.4%, its third straight weekly gain.
Telecommunications stocks fell, weighing on the communication services sector, after a report that SpaceX was seeking thousands of cell sites for a fourth wireless carrier.
Shares of AT&T and T-Mobile both sank nearly 8% while Verizon shed 1.2%. SpaceX shares rose 1.9%.
US cell tower operators gained, with Crown Castle up 9% and American Tower up 4%.

The energy sector rose 2.5%, hitting a record high. Brent crude hit its highest level since late April, after Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concern over further disruption to energy supplies from the Middle East.
American Express shares fell 3.7%, weighing on the Dow. The company raised its profit forecast as it also announced plans to eliminate 5% of its workforce.
SLB shares rose 7% after the oilfield services provider beat Wall Street estimates for third-quarter profit.

Data from the University of Michigan showed US consumer sentiment edged down near a record low in October, as rising prices because of the Middle East conflict soured households’ views of the economy.

Market focus remains on the earnings season, with robust corporate profit growth underpinning gains for major equity indexes this year. S&P 500 companies are on track to have increased earnings by more than 32% in the third quarter, according to LSEG IBES data.

The Fed is expected to keep interest rates steady when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, but investors will be eager for clues about whether the US central bank will hike rates at its December meeting. Wall Street is also increasingly focused on the Nov 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the US Congress.
Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.72-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. On the Nasdaq, declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.57-to-1 ratio.
The S&P 500 posted 18 new 52-week highs and 8 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 74 new highs and 334 new lows.
Volume on US exchanges was 15.4 billion shares, compared with the 17.2 billion average over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

cna.headline: Majority of parents and youths prefer tiered access to social media over outright ban: MDDI
cna.teaser: Excessive use of social media ranked among the top concerns raised by more than 2,000 parents and youths in an engagement by the Ministry of Digital Development and Information.
fullText: SINGAPORE: About 80 per cent of parents and nearly 70 per cent of youths support tiered access to social media over an outright ban, according to findings from the Ministry of Digital Development and Information’s (MDDI) engagement with over 2,000 parents and youths.

The ministry said the findings reinforce the government’s proposed approach of age-appropriate access, alongside platform adjustments to let young people benefit from technology with stronger protections.
It intends to introduce legislation next year focused on age assurance and safer design of social media for teenagers.

Under the approach, platforms would have to put in place effective age assurance measures for young users and make their services safer by design , the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) said.
The findings come as more countries have enforced social media bans for children.

Indonesia was the first country in Southeast Asia to restrict children under 16 from using social media in March this year. Malaysia soon followed in June, enforcing rules barring children under 16 from having social media accounts.
The findings come from MDDI's engagements with parents and youths between June and August 2026 on young people's social media use, online risks and a tiered approach to social media access.

The engagements comprised focus group discussions, school dialogues and a survey on CrowdTaskSG. Community partners including TOUCH Community Services, Fei Yue Community Services, YouthTechSG and Singapore Children’s Society also provided perspectives.

Neither parents nor youths favoured an outright ban on social media for children, the ministry said. Both groups felt education, digital literacy and graduated access would be “more sustainable” than blanket restrictions.

Parents felt children should be introduced to online platforms gradually so they learn to navigate social media in a safer environment. Some youths said overly restrictive measures risk a “forbidden fruit” effect, which makes social media more appealing.

Both groups felt children aged zero to six should have no access, while those aged seven to 15 should have age-appropriate access. Youths generally supported greater access to social media from age 16, seeing young people as more mature and better able to manage their use independently, while parents continued to support age-appropriate access.
MDDI said some parents and youths also expressed caution against relying solely on age to gauge maturity.

Close to 80 per cent of parents agreed that age verification or age estimation should be implemented. Verification relies on a verified source of identity documentation and is seen as more reliable and easier to enforce, while estimation uses artificial intelligence and facial age analysis to determine a user’s likely age.
At the same time, parents also emphasised the importance of safeguarding privacy and not collecting excessive personal data.

Both parents and youths ranked excessive use of social media among their top concerns. About 84 per cent of parents ranked exposure to inappropriate content among their top concerns, a concern that ranked lower among youths.
Both groups also raised concerns that features such as autoplay, infinite scrolling and targeted feeds encourage compulsive use, MDDI said.

Parents generally supported daily screen-time limits but preferred the flexibility to adjust them to their children’s needs. The top three proposed default safeguards were disabling autoplay, disabling direct messaging and implementing a daily screen-time limit.

Youths were concerned that fixed and rigid limits could restrict legitimate uses such as schoolwork and extracurricular activities. While there was broad support for disabling algorithmic feeds, some saw value in their ability to surface educational content.

“In general, many parents expressed desire to retain some agency and flexibility over how safeguards were implemented, particularly where measures such as autoplay and daily time limits might need to be tailored to their children's developmental needs, maturity levels and family circumstances,” MDDI said.

IMDA is also partnering with government-supported preschools on lessons about digital habits , built around four key actions: setting boundaries online, thinking before acting, reporting inappropriate content, and parental engagement and support.

The curriculum was first piloted with more than 100 Kindergarten 2 students from E-Bridge preschool. It will be rolled out across all E-Bridge preschool centres from December, reaching close to 3,000 Kindergarten 1 and 2 students across 30 centres.

Skool4Kidz preschool also delivered the curriculum to 800 Kindergarten 2 children across 35 of its centres in September. IMDA said it will continue to engage the Early Childhood Development Agency and reach out to more preschool operators next year.
Parents and families can also access digital parenting resources on the Digital for Life portal, it said.

mom.headline: Additional Guidance for Employers on Use of 1-Hour PM2.5 Readings to Protect Outdoor Workers During Haze
mom.teaser: 1 The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) has issued new guidance on how employers should adjust outdoor work based on the 1-hour PM2.5 readings. This complements the existing guidance based on the PSI forecast, and helps employers respond within the day as air quality changes.

listening.title: Singapore Expands EV Charging Infrastructure Across Residential Estates
listening.transcript: Singapore is accelerating its transition towards greener transportation by expanding electric vehicle charging stations across residential heartlands. The Land Transport Authority announced that thousands of new charging points will be installed in public carparks over the coming months. This initiative aims to reassure drivers about charging accessibility and encourage faster adoption of clean-energy cars. Officials emphasized that building a robust ecosystem is essential to meeting the nation's 2030 sustainability targets.

economistArticle.title: Defusing the China Shock: Rethinking the Cost of Globalisation
paras: For two decades, the consensus among Western economists was that free trade generated broad prosperity, even if localized disruptions occurred. That consensus shattered in 2016 following landmark research on the so-called China shock. Economists David Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon Hanson demonstrated that rapid Chinese import penetration after its entry into the World Trade Organisation severely damaged manufacturing communities across America. The paper fundamentally altered the political debate, providing empirical backing for rising protectionism.

Now, fresh academic literature is attempting to re-evaluate those explosive findings. Newer studies suggest that while initial employment losses in specific manufacturing regions were genuine, the broader nationwide remedies and offset effects were underestimated. Researchers argue that lower consumer prices and growth in service-sector employment provided significant economic buffers that diluted the aggregate damage across national economies over time.

Furthermore, critics of the original thesis contend that technology, rather than Chinese competition, played a primary role in displacing factory labor. Automation and digital supply chain management were already reshaping industrial landscapes long before Beijing became the world factory floor. Distinguishing between technological obsolescence and trade competition remains a complex empirical challenge for macroeconomic researchers.

This ongoing scholastic battle carries profound real-world policy implications. If trade with emerging economies was indeed the central culprit for industrial decline, aggressive tariffs and reshoring directives appear justified. Conversely, if trade friction was merely a secondary symptom of broader technological shifts, protectionist barriers will simply raise living costs without restoring factory jobs.

As geopolitical tensions escalate, policymakers must navigate these competing economic interpretations carefully. Overreacting with sweeping trade restrictions risks strangling economic dynamism and reigniting inflationary pressures. Defusing the hyperbole around the China shock is therefore not merely an academic exercise, but an urgent prerequisite for crafting sound economic policy in an interconnected world.
economistArticle.cn:
二十年来，西方经济学家的共识是，自由贸易即使造成局部阵痛，也能带来广泛繁荣。这一共识在2016年关于所谓“中国冲击”的里程碑式研究出炉后被打破。经济学家戴维·奥特尔、戴维·多恩和戈登·汉森证明，中国加入世界贸易组织后快速的进口渗透，严重破坏了全美制造业社区。这篇论文从根本上改变了政治辩论，为日益抬头的保护主义提供了实证支持。

如今，最新的学术文献正在尝试重新评估这些爆发性的研究结论。近期的研究表明，虽然特定制造业地区的初期就业损失是真实的，但更广泛的全国性补救措施和抵消效应却被低估了。研究人员指出，更低廉的商品价格以及服务业就业的增长提供了显著的经济缓冲，随着时间的推移稀释了对国家经济的总体损害。

此外，原始论点的批评者主张，技术而非中国的竞争，才是淘汰工厂劳动力的主因。早在北京成为“世界工厂”之前，自动化和数字供应链管理就已经在重塑工业格局。区分技术淘汰与贸易竞争对宏观经济研究人员而言仍是一个复杂的实证挑战。

这场持续的学术争论具有深远的现实政策意义。如果与新兴经济体的贸易确实是工业衰退的核心罪魁祸首，那么激进的关税和产能回流指令似乎顺理成章。反之，如果贸易摩擦只是更广泛技术变革的次要症状，那么保护主义壁垒只会提高生活成本，却无法恢复工厂岗位。

随着地缘政治紧张局势的加剧，政策制定者必须审慎应对这些相互竞争的经济解释。采取一刀切的贸易限制措施进行过度反应，可能会扼杀经济活力并重新引发通胀压力。因此，化解围绕“中国冲击”的夸大说法不仅是一项学术研究，更是当今互联世界中制定合理经济政策的迫切前提。

gems.why: This sentence uses a clear framing technique ('Distinguishing between X and Y remains Z') to balance two competing academic hypotheses, offering a sophisticated structure for analytical writing. 句子采用了清晰的对比表述结构（‘区分X与Y仍是Z’），平衡了两种不同的学术假说，是严谨分析类写作的优秀示范。
